base_properties.human_readable: Organization Floor in Democratic Policy Markets

stakeholders.name: organized_labor_unions
stakeholders.situation: Maintain institutional infrastructure to aggregate member preferences, negotiate with political actors, deliver votes and campaign resources, and punish defection. The organization floor makes their preferences tradable while unorganized workers' preferences remain non-transactable, creating systematic advantage in policy markets regardless of preference intensity.

stakeholders.name: professional_associations
stakeholders.situation: Convert diffuse professional interests into concentrated policy influence through credentialing, lobbying infrastructure, and campaign contribution bundling. The floor ensures their organized voice carries weight while unorganized practitioners in the same field remain politically invisible.

stakeholders.name: industry_coalitions
stakeholders.situation: Pool resources across firms to maintain permanent lobbying presence, fund policy research, and coordinate campaign contributions. The organization floor converts their collective preferences into tradable political assets while atomized small businesses and consumers face prohibitive transaction costs.

stakeholders.name: political_party_machines
stakeholders.situation: Operate the policy market itself, setting the terms of trade and determining which organized blocs get access. They benefit from the floor because it simplifies transaction costs: negotiating with a dozen organized blocs is cheaper than aggregating millions of individual preferences. The floor is the market structure they administer.

stakeholders.name: unorganized_mass_publics
stakeholders.situation: Hold intense preferences on issues like consumer protection, environmental quality, or public goods provision, but lack the organizational infrastructure to make those preferences tradable. Their votes matter in elections but their policy preferences are systematically discounted in legislative bargaining because they cannot credibly promise delivery or punishment.

stakeholders.name: diffuse_consumer_interests
stakeholders.situation: Bear concentrated costs from policies that benefit organized producer groups (tariffs, occupational licensing, regulatory capture). Each individual's stake is too small to justify organization costs, so their preferences remain below the transactability threshold even when aggregate welfare losses are large.

stakeholders.name: geographically_dispersed_minorities
stakeholders.situation: Face systematic underrepresentation because their population is distributed across many districts rather than concentrated. The organization floor compounds this: they cannot easily form the dense local networks that enable organization, so their preferences remain non-transactable even when intensity is high.

stakeholders.name: political_scientists
stakeholders.situation: Study the organization floor as an empirical regularity in democratic systems. They debate whether it is a natural law emerging from transaction costs and collective action problems, or a constructed constraint that benefits organized interests at the expense of mass publics.

stakeholders.name: institutional_reformers
stakeholders.situation: Propose mechanisms to lower the organization floor: participatory budgeting, citizen assemblies, quadratic voting, digital organizing platforms. They are systematically excluded from policy design because the organized blocs who benefit from the current floor control access to the legislative agenda.

six_questions.coordination_function: Solves the transaction cost problem in democratic policy markets by creating a stable set of organized counterparties that political actors can negotiate with, rather than attempting to aggregate millions of individual preferences in real time.
six_questions.transfer_function: Systematically transfers policy influence from unorganized mass publics to organized blocs, regardless of preference intensity or population size. Organized groups capture policy rents; unorganized groups bear diffuse costs.
six_questions.absent_voices: Institutional reformers who would lower the organization threshold through participatory mechanisms are excluded from agenda-setting because the organized blocs who benefit from the current floor control legislative access. Unorganized publics are structurally absent by definition.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: Political scientists and organized blocs argue the floor would re-emerge immediately from transaction cost economics — any attempt to aggregate unorganized preferences would recreate the same threshold. Reformers argue digital infrastructure and participatory institutions could lower the floor substantially, making currently non-transactable preferences tradable.
six_questions.founding_problem: Early democratic systems faced prohibitive costs in aggregating individual preferences into coherent policy demands. Organization solved this by creating stable intermediaries who could negotiate on behalf of blocs.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Organized blocs attest the transaction cost problem is permanent and the floor is necessary. Political scientists outside the benefiting organizations are divided: some cite transaction cost theory as supporting the floor's necessity; others point to successful participatory experiments (Porto Alegre, Taiwan's vTaiwan, digital petition systems) as evidence the floor can be lowered with institutional innovation. No consensus exists outside the beneficiary set.

commentary.narrative_context:
The organization floor in democratic policy markets describes a structural threshold below which mass preferences cannot be converted into tradable political assets. This constraint appears as a natural law to most observers — an inevitable consequence of transaction costs and collective action problems in large-scale democracies. However, the systematic presence of identifiable beneficiaries (organized labor, professional associations, industry coalitions, political party machines) who capture policy influence at the expense of unorganized mass publics triggers false summit evaluation. The constraint is CLAIMED as mountain (emerges from transaction cost economics) while the metrics describe moderate extraction that has accumulated over time as organized blocs have learned to exploit the floor. The claim/metric divergence is the measurement.

KEY AGENTS (by structural relationship):
- Organized labor unions: Primary beneficiary (organized/mobile) — preferences made tradable by organization
- Professional associations: Primary beneficiary (organized/mobile) — convert diffuse interests into concentrated influence
- Industry coalitions: Primary beneficiary (powerful/arbitrage) — pool resources to maintain permanent lobbying presence
- Political party machines: Agenda setter (institutional/constrained) — administer the policy market, benefit from simplified transaction costs
- Unorganized mass publics: Primary victim (powerless/trapped) — intense preferences remain non-transactable
- Diffuse consumer interests: Primary victim (powerless/trapped) — bear concentrated costs from organized producer policies
- Geographically dispersed minorities: Primary victim (powerless/identity_locked) — distribution pattern prevents organization
- Political scientists: Analytical observer — debate natural law vs. constructed constraint
- Institutional reformers: Excluded (moderate/constrained) — propose floor-lowering mechanisms, blocked by organized beneficiaries
commentary.logic_rationale: Extraction is moderate (0.42) because the floor systematically transfers policy influence from unorganized to organized groups, but the transfer is mediated through genuine transaction cost reduction rather than pure coercion. Suppression is moderate-low (0.38) because the constraint operates through structural barriers to organization rather than active prohibition — unorganized groups are not forbidden from organizing, but face prohibitive costs. Theater ratio is low (0.22) because the coordination function is real: organized blocs do solve genuine aggregation problems, even as they capture rents from the solution. Accessibility collapse is high (0.78) because once you understand transaction cost economics, alternative mechanisms for aggregating preferences appear prohibitively expensive. Resistance is moderate-low (0.31) because most actors accept the floor as natural, though reformers contest it. The temporal measurements show gradual extraction accumulation as organized blocs have learned to exploit the floor more effectively over time.
commentary.directionality_logic: Organized blocs (labor unions, professional associations, industry coalitions) are structural beneficiaries: the floor makes their preferences tradable while competitors remain below the threshold. They sit near d=0.15-0.25 (beneficiary end). Political party machines are agenda setters who benefit from simplified transaction costs but are also constrained by the floor's rigidity; they sit near d=0.35 (weakly beneficiary). Unorganized mass publics, diffuse consumer interests, and geographically dispersed minorities are the targets: their preferences are systematically discounted regardless of intensity. They sit near d=0.85-0.95 (target end, with identity-locked minorities at the high end). Political scientists are analytical observers at d=0.5. The engine derives these positions from the beneficiary/victim declarations and exit options.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the organized blocs' perspective, the floor is a natural law emerging from transaction cost economics — they built the infrastructure to cross it, and unorganized groups could do the same. From the unorganized victims' perspective, the floor is a constructed barrier that organized interests defend to preserve their advantage. From the party machines' perspective, the floor is the market structure they inherited and must work within. The engine computes these divergent classifications from the structural data: beneficiaries with mobile exit see coordination; victims with trapped exit see extraction.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The false summit machinery prevents mislabeling this as pure extraction. The coordination function is real: organized blocs do solve genuine transaction cost problems in democratic policy markets. The floor enables stable, repeated negotiation rather than chaotic preference aggregation. However, the systematic presence of beneficiaries who capture policy rents, combined with rising extraction over time and moderate suppression of alternatives, triggers FSM evaluation. The constraint is not a snare (the coordination function is genuine), but it is also not a pure mountain (identifiable actors benefit from its persistence and resist floor-lowering innovations). The omega variables document the irreducible uncertainty about whether the floor's height is determined by transaction cost economics or by organized interests' defensive action.

omegas.question: Is the organization floor's height determined by inherent transaction costs in preference aggregation, or by organized blocs' active defense against floor-lowering innovations?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Natural experiments from jurisdictions that implement participatory mechanisms (citizen assemblies, digital platforms, participatory budgeting): if the floor lowers substantially without organized bloc consent, defensive maintenance is the dominant factor. If attempted innovations fail to lower the floor despite institutional support, transaction costs dominate.
omegas.impact: If transaction costs dominate, the constraint is a genuine mountain and the extraction is the minimum price of coordination. If defensive maintenance dominates, the constraint is a tangled rope where organized blocs extract rents by preventing institutional innovation.
omegas.description: Whether the floor's height is natural law or constructed barrier

omegas.question: Can digital organizing platforms and participatory institutions lower the organization floor to make currently non-transactable preferences tradable, or do they simply recreate the same threshold at a different level?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparative analysis of digital democracy experiments (vTaiwan, Decidim, participatory budgeting platforms): measure whether unorganized preferences that were previously non-transactable become tradable, or whether new organized intermediaries emerge to capture the same rents.
omegas.impact: If digital infrastructure genuinely lowers the floor, the current threshold is a technological artifact rather than a natural law. If new intermediaries emerge to capture the same rents, the floor is a structural feature of democratic systems regardless of technology.
omegas.description: Whether technological innovation can lower the organization threshold

omegas.question: Is there a fundamental tradeoff between preference intensity and organizational capacity in democratic systems, such that intense but unorganized preferences must remain non-transactable?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Theoretical analysis of mechanism design in democratic systems, combined with empirical study of cases where intense unorganized preferences did become tradable (social movements, moral panics, crisis mobilization).
omegas.impact: If the tradeoff is fundamental, the floor is a natural law and attempts to lower it will fail or create worse pathologies. If the tradeoff is contingent on institutional design, the floor is a constructed constraint that can be redesigned.
omegas.description: Whether the intensity-organization tradeoff is fundamental or contingent
